universe_context: In January 2024, Delaware Court of Chancery Vice Chancellor Kathaleen McCormick ruled in Tornetta v. Musk to rescind Elon Musk's roughly $56 billion Tesla pay package, which the board and shareholders had originally approved in 2018. McCormick found the package resulted from a deeply flawed, non-independent process: Musk exerted outsized influence over the compensation committee and negotiations, several of the directors involved had close personal or financial ties to him, and the proxy statement given to shareholders before their 2018 vote contained materially misleading disclosures about how independent that process really was. The ruling was widely covered as a rebuke of Tesla's board and corporate-governance practices, not a validation of them. In June 2024, Tesla shareholders held a re-vote and re-approved the same pay package by a large majority, but in December 2024 McCormick declined to reverse her original ruling on the basis of that re-vote, holding the package voided regardless. Musk and Tesla have appealed the ruling to the Delaware Supreme Court.
key_facts: In January 2024, Vice Chancellor Kathaleen McCormick of the Delaware Court of Chancery rescinded (voided) Elon Musk's roughly $56 billion Tesla pay package in the case Tornetta v. Musk.

McCormick's ruling found the compensation process was not independent -- Musk had outsized influence over the board/committee and several directors had close ties to him -- and that the 2018 proxy disclosures to shareholders were misleading.
The ruling was a rebuke of Tesla's governance process, not praise or validation of it as a best-practice model.
Tesla shareholders re-approved the same pay package in a June 2024 re-vote, but McCormick declined in December 2024 to reverse her ruling based on that re-vote.
Musk and Tesla have appealed the ruling to the Delaware Supreme Court.
